job.style: a passage rich in numbers, dates or measurements

response.passage: The Earth is a fascinating planet that performs two distinct movements. First, it rotates on its axis, an imaginary line connecting the North and South Poles, completing one full spin in approximately 24 hours. This rotation creates the cycle of day and night as different parts of the Earth face the Sun. While the Earth spins, it also travels around the Sun in an elliptical orbit, a journey known as revolution. This trip takes about 365 and a quarter days to complete. Because we cannot count a quarter day every year, we add an extra day to our calendar every four years, creating a leap year. Interestingly, the Earth's distance from the Sun changes throughout the year, but this does not cause our seasons. Instead, seasons occur because the Earth is tilted at an angle of 23.5 degrees on its axis as it revolves. When the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, it experiences summer, regardless of whether the Earth is at its closest or farthest point from the Sun. The Sun remains stationary at the center of our solar system, while the Earth moves around it, ensuring that light reaches different regions at different times of the year.
response.summary: The Earth rotates on an imaginary axis to create day and night while revolving around the Sun to cause seasons. Its tilt, rather than its distance from the Sun, determines the changing seasons throughout the year.
